# Internet Force 1995–1996 Historical Archive

Website: https://pippocom.github.io/internetforce-1995/
Repository: https://github.com/pippocom/internetforce-1995
Author and curator: Marco Iannacone
Author website: https://pippo.com/me/

## About this archive

This site is a historical and technical reconstruction of Internet Force, an Italian Internet Service Provider founded in Milan in 1995 and active during 1995–1996.

The archive preserves and documents original technical material from the provider, including surviving system and network configurations, operational documentation, software, customer materials, historical network maps, email and Usenet material, company and commercial documents, photographs, public archival traces, and other artifacts from the period.

The purpose of the project is not simply to preserve old files. It is to reconstruct how a small commercial Internet provider of the mid-1990s actually worked: its network architecture, Unix systems, dial-up access, routing, DNS, email, authentication, web services, security, monitoring, Point of Presence infrastructure, commercial services, customer onboarding, and day-to-day operations.

## Author and historical role

Marco Iannacone is the author and curator of this archive.

At Internet Force, Marco Iannacone built and operated the provider's technical infrastructure as its sole system and network administrator. His work included the Unix service platform, networking, routing, authentication, Internet services, monitoring, security infrastructure, POP configuration and operational management.

This historical reconstruction is based on original materials preserved by Marco Iannacone together with his direct first-person testimony as the person who designed, configured and operated the infrastructure.

More information about the author:
https://pippo.com/me/

## Why this archive exists

Internet infrastructure from the early commercial Internet era is unusually fragile as historical evidence.

Small Internet providers were built from Unix hosts, routers, modems, configuration files, scripts, printed manuals, email, Usenet discussions and the practical knowledge of the people who operated them. Much of this material was never formally archived and was easily lost when companies closed, hardware was discarded and systems were replaced.

Internet Force provides a compact example of how an independent ISP was actually assembled and operated in 1995, during the transition from an academic and specialist Internet to mass commercial access.

Preserving the archive therefore serves several purposes:

- documenting the technical architecture of an early Italian commercial ISP;
- preserving original configurations and operational artifacts together with first-person historical reconstruction;
- showing how Internet services were deployed and administered before today's cloud platforms and managed infrastructure;
- documenting what Internet access and related services were commercially sold to individuals and businesses;
- preserving the engineering practices, tools, customer materials and operational culture of the period;
- connecting the recovered archive with contemporary and immediately subsequent public traces from Usenet, the Wayback Machine and public company records;
- providing material for researchers, historians, engineers, students and anyone studying the development of the commercial Internet.

This is intended as technical and digital archaeology, not nostalgia.

## Main areas

### Narrative documentation
https://pippocom.github.io/internetforce-1995/docs/

Technical reconstruction of the architecture, services, POPs, operations, security, authentication, networking, monitoring and shutdown/migration history.

### Systems
https://pippocom.github.io/internetforce-1995/systems/

System-specific documentation and surviving configurations for routers, Unix hosts, firewall, development systems, POPs and related infrastructure.

### Historical artifacts
https://pippocom.github.io/internetforce-1995/artifacts/

Original manuals, customer materials, software, network monitoring material, email, Usenet posts, photographs, inventories, company and commercial documents, public Web traces and other recovered material.

### Publications
https://github.com/pippocom/internetforce-1995/tree/main/publications

Articles and publications connected with the reconstruction of the Internet Force archive, including Marco Iannacone's 2026 Codemotion article published together with the repository.

https://pippocom.github.io/internetforce-1995/site/index.en.html

Interactive historical network maps and a browser for technical documentation and surviving configuration files.

### Italian interactive archive
https://pippocom.github.io/internetforce-1995/site/index.html

Italian-language entry point to the interactive archive.

## Internet Force interactive network maps

Internet Force was one of Italy's early commercial Internet service providers, active in 1995–1996. Its structured routed-IP architecture was technologically advanced for a small ISP of the period. System & network administrator Marco Iannacone contributed directly to designing, building and operating the infrastructure, drawing in part on technical training with Xpert Unix Systems in Israel. Internet Force was also the first provider to host Iannacone's pippo.com domain in 1995. The interactive maps reconstruct the historical network from surviving original technical material, including network and system configurations, monitoring maps, DNS records and Cisco configurations.

- Italian interactive maps: https://pippocom.github.io/internetforce-1995/site/index.html
- English interactive maps: https://pippocom.github.io/internetforce-1995/site/index.en.html

## Codemotion article

Marco Iannacone published the article *Archeologia di un ISP: come funzionava davvero un Internet provider nel 1995* with Codemotion in October 2026 together with the Internet Force 1995–1996 repository and its data. It describes the recovery of the archive, the architecture and operation of Internet Force, dial-up connectivity, Unix and Cisco infrastructure, the Welcome Kit, day-to-day work and the surviving historical material.

- Italian Codemotion edition: https://www.codemotion.com/magazine/it/dev-life-it/storie/archeologia-di-un-isp-come-funzionava-davvero-un-internet-provider-nel-1995/
- English Codemotion edition: https://www.codemotion.com/magazine/dev-life/stories/the-archaeology-of-an-isp-how-an-internet-provider-really-worked-in-1995/
- Repository-preserved PDF and publication metadata: https://github.com/pippocom/internetforce-1995/tree/main/publications/codemotion-2026

## Business services and 1996 Web hosting

The Internet Force Business Price List dated 15 June 1996 documents a structured business offer in addition to individual Internet access: static IP addressing, LAN dial-up, 19.2 and 64 Kbps LAN connectivity, domain registration, DNS backup, HTML page production, Web hosting and specialised support.

Web hosting was sold in 1 MB, 5 MB and 10 MB tiers, with larger quantities quoted individually. These sizes reflect the scale of business websites in 1996 and the constraints of users commonly accessing pages over 28.8 kbit/s dial-up connections.

Price-list documentation:
https://github.com/pippocom/internetforce-1995/tree/main/artifacts/company/business-services-price-list-1996

## Customer Welcome Kit

The customer Welcome Kit included a printed manual, installation floppies, Internet client software and the Easy! launcher developed by Marco Iannacone. The archive also preserves photographs of the original version 1.0 physical packaging and labelled floppies, supplied in 2026 by Internet Force founding shareholder Pascal Schait.

Welcome Kit archive:
https://github.com/pippocom/internetforce-1995/tree/main/artifacts/customer-welcome-kit

## Public traces and contemporary sources

The repository also records public traces that can be read alongside the recovered technical archive:

- Google Groups screenshots show 1996 Usenet conversations containing `@internetforce.com` and `@intf.com` addresses across unrelated newsgroups. A captured search for `Internetforce.com` displayed 208 conversations; this is a conversation count, not a distinct-user count.
- A 22 March 1996 Usenet post by Marco Iannacone identifies him as Internet Force's System Administrator while discussing a proposed e-mail/GSM-SMS gateway.
- The 5 June 1997 Wayback snapshot of `internetforce.com` shows Enter after the central-services migration.
- The 3 May 1997 Wayback snapshot of `pesaro.com` shows autonomous Pesaro Point while still displaying the Internet Force I.S.P. mark.
- The public Italian Business Register record shows a Milan local unit at Via Plana 20, matching the 1996 Business Price List's “Sede Operativa”.

Documentation:
https://github.com/pippocom/internetforce-1995/blob/main/docs/26-public-traces-and-contemporary-sources.en.md

Artifacts:
https://github.com/pippocom/internetforce-1995/tree/main/artifacts/usenet/google-groups
